en: The *Sāmānyadūṣaṇadikprasāritā* composed by the scholar Aśoka. By those who have postulated a universal (*sāmānya*) that is pervasive, eternal, and unitary—
The absence of that [doubt] is established for them through the severing of the knot of delusion.
How is this understood?

We say that it is because there is an absence of any proving evidence (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) and the presence of subverting evidence (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) to maintain that a universal (*sāmānya*), which is the basis for the production of a single cognition and term amidst moments perceived by direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) as mutually distinct, is not respected by the wise.
For instance, this inference which is called "general proof" by others is as follows:
"Whatever cognition has a recurring form (anugatākāra) is based upon a recurring entity, just as the cognition 'garland' regarding many flowers [is based on the recurring entity 'garland-ness'].

However, since there exists a recurring cognition regarding individual effects and so forth that lack mutual contact, the body of this argument is afflicted by the fault of being inconclusive (anaikāntika); therefore, it is not capable of proving the existence of that [recurring universal].
For instance, when there are many cooks, there arises a conceptual cognition that apprehends them as having a single form, namely, "cook, cook";
yet no single entity that is common to them exists.
For if such an entity did exist, the undesirable consequence would be unavoidable: that such a cognition would have arisen even earlier.
If it is argued that this fault does not apply because the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), which depend on assistance through action, manifest the universal (*sāmānya*), we say:
this is not so. Because eternal things cannot have any excellence added to them, it is impossible for them to depend on auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) that provide no assistance.
Alternatively, if there were a superiority [in the action], then because the body perishes at every moment, how could there be action? Thus the fault is difficult to avoid.
Nor is it a valid argument to say that the objection of inconclusiveness does not apply because the uniform cognition of "cook" among cooks is based on action;
for since actions differ with each individual instance, they cannot logically serve as the basis for such a [uniform] cognition.

If individual instances were the basis for a cognition of a non-different form even though they are themselves different, then the existence of such a state for those individuals would not be prevented by the king’s rod [of punishment].
Consequently, one would not even have to accept a universal (*sāmānya*).
Thus, by adopting this root-subverting position, the "Beloved of the Gods" has acted most favorably toward himself!

By this very same reasoning, one who postulates that the relationship between action and its factors (kāraka) is based on a non-differentiated cognition is refuted. Furthermore, it should not be thought that the uniform cognition occurring with respect to cooks is caused by the universal (jāti) "cooking-action" (*pākakriyātva*); for a universal residing in one thing cannot be the cause for the production of a cognition regarding a different thing.
Because it would lead to an over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*).

It might be argued: "By the force of the relation of inherence-in-that-which-is-inherent (*samavetasamavāya*), the generality of the action of cooking produces a reflective cognition (*parāmarśapratyaya*) of a non-different form with respect to cooks; therefore, the aforementioned fault does not apply.
This too is without substance.

Since action itself is impossible once it has been discarded immediately after its arising, that universal [of action] does not reside in the action because the action has perished; nor does it reside in the agent, precisely because of the absence of the action. Thus, it lacks even a connection through a connected entity (sambandhasambandha) and is therefore not the cause of a non-differentiated cognition.
Consequently, it remains established that this inference is incapable of proving the existence of a universal, as it is vitiated by the fault of being inconclusive (anaikāntika).
For this reason as well, this inference does not establish the existence of a universal:

for just as entities such as brindled cows (*śābaleya*) and others, despite having mutually distinct natures, assist that single intended common form by means of a certain specific nature— characterized by the restriction to a single effect— which has come about through the power of their own causes,
and this occurs without any other further universal, otherwise there would follow the consequence of an infinite regress.

In that case, let those [individuals] produce that single synthetic cognition; what is the use of postulating a separate universal (*sāmānya*) as an intermediate obstacle, which possesses a distinct nature?
Now, it might be argued that all entities possess specific, restricted potencies (*pratiniyata-śakti*).
This must necessarily be admitted even by those who deny the existence of universals; otherwise, why would a rice seed produce only a rice sprout and not a *kodrava* sprout?
In response to this objection, what else remains to be said here apart from the nature of existence (*bhāvaprakṛti*)?
This answer is not something that even our forest-dwelling opponents have swallowed;

for we too are capable of saying this: although there is no difference in the distinction between the powers and their manifestations, the universal alone is capable of producing that single cognition.
Alas, this is an unsurpassed calamity of faults: even while entering into the fault of a [wrong] view, your honor does not perceive yourself by means of yourself.

For instance, once the causal relationship between a rice seed and its sprout has been understood—based on perception and non-perception—it can be stated that the rice seed is capable of producing a rice sprout, but not a *kodrava* sprout.

The relationship of beneficiary and benefactor between the universal and its possessor has not been ascertained from any means of valid cognition (pramāṇa). Therefore, how can this response, being stated, possess any merit? Enough with this futile persistence;
for the wise do not engage in the conventional treatment of something as non-existent merely because of the absence of a proving means of cognition.
Therefore, let this inference which establishes its non-existence, as set forth by us, be considered: whatever,
being characterized by perceptibility, is not perceived, that should be treated as non-existent by discerning people,
just like a lotus in the sky.
Furthermore, since a universal that meets the conditions for perception is not perceived anywhere, this is a case of the non-perception of an essential nature (*svabhāvānupalabdhi*).
Nor should one object here by raising the charge of the fault of being unestablished (*asiddha*).
For if there were an unestablished reason here, it would have to be so either in its own form or in its qualification.
In that regard, the first [alternative] is not possible,
because non-apprehension is admitted to have the nature of the apprehension of something else,

and since its own nature is directly realized through self-cognizing perception (*svasaṃvedana-pratyakṣa*), how could there be any room for the fault of the unestablished nature of the subject (*svarūpāsiddha*)?
Now it is argued that self-awareness itself is not possible,
because of the contradiction of an action operating upon itself;
for indeed, a blade cannot cut that very same blade by means of that very same blade.
"Just as that very tip of a finger is touched by that same tip of a finger," therefore this reason is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*).
This [argument] merely reveals the manifestation of a complete lack of understanding regarding the meaning of the term "self-cognition" (*svasaṃvedana*).
For instance, a cognition arises as excluded from [objects such as] a jar, silver, or a blue lotus.
Therefore, its very arising in the form of awareness is called its self-cognition, just like light.
This is not so, because of the absence of the relationship between action, agent, and object;
for it is logically impossible for a single entity that lacks constituent parts to possess a threefold nature.
Indeed, just as light, which does not depend on another illuminator, is said to be the illuminator of itself while it is shining.
Likewise, knowledge as well, manifesting independently of another cognition, is said to be the manifestation of itself.
Therefore, this is the ultimate truth:
it is not logical that knowledge is cognized by another cognition, nor is it said to be uncognized.

Furthermore, when the intended meaning of the term *svasaṃvedana* (self-cognition) is taken in its literal sense, there is nothing further to be said; how then could there be any occasion for the aforementioned faults? Nor can the charge of the non-establishment of the qualification (*viśeṣaṇāsiddhi*) be raised, because the opponent themselves accepts that the universal (*sāmānya*) possesses the conditions for apprehension (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāpta*).
Or, if this is not accepted, then by the power of a universal (sāmānya), there would be no cognition or verbal designation with a recurring form in respect to things such as "kuleya" and so forth.

For when the occurrence of a cognition or a name takes place in relation to something, there can be no comprehension of that thing if its basis is not perceived, just as in the case of a staff-bearer.
As for that which was illuminated by Uddyotakara:

Do you accept a universal (sāmānya), or not? If you do accept it, how can you deny it? If, on the other hand, you do not accept it, then because that [universal] is unestablished, the reason (hetu) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished locus (āśrayāsiddha).
This appears to be the manifestation of his ignorance regarding the true nature of the subject (*dharmin*).
For we do not accept the universal (*sāmānya*) as the subject in its external form;

rather, it is employed as the subject because it is a form of cognition (*jñānākāra*) superimposed upon an external object, which arises from the maturation of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) deposited by the experience of both existence and non-existence, and which belongs to those who are intent only upon the internal [mind].
And since that [subject] is established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanapratyakṣa*), it cannot be rejected.
Therefore, those who are established upon this subject (*dharmin*) deliberate upon its existence or non-existence:
"Is this subject—the object appearing in conceptual cognition through a general term (*sāmānyaśabda*)—based on an external universal (*sāmānya*) postulated by others, or is it not?"
When its external non-appropriation is the probandum, non-perception is the reason;
however, its very non-existence is not being proven,
because that would entail the consequence of using a word whose referent is that [non-existent thing].
And when such a subject (*dharmin*) is intended to be expressed, how can there be the fault of the unestablished locus (*āśrayāsiddhi*)?
As for what is said—

that because its nature is established by the means of valid cognition of direct perception (*pratyakṣapramāṇa*), this reason (*hetu*) is indeed unestablished (*asiddha*) with respect to the universal (*sāmānya*)— [that is not so].
That is incorrect, because it does not appear in its own form;
for this indeed is the perceptuality of perception: that it presents its own form to its own cognition.
Furthermore, this [universal] is like a buyer who pays no price; it neither reveals its own nature nor seeks to accept perceptibility.

For we do not perceive, at the time when the distinct individuals such as the brindled cow (*śābaleya*) appear unmixed with one another, any other recurring entity that is different from them—just as one does not perceive a necklace upon living beings.
Since the cognition of a universal such as "spottedness" (śāvaleyasāmānya) is unestablished,
how could we deceive ourselves by means of our own [intellect] through the postulation of something unseen?
Thus, the reason is not unestablished.
Nor does the suspicion of inconclusiveness (anaikāntikatā) fall within the range of possibility, because no occurrence [of the reason] in the dissimilar class (vipakṣa) is observed,
and because its presence in what is not the similar class (asapakṣa) is not perceived.
Let there be no common inconclusiveness;

however, the state of having a doubtful exclusion from the dissimilar class (sandigdhavipakṣavyāvṛttikatā) cannot be prevented from spreading, since no necessary connection (pratibandha) is observed. Therefore, this statement is not for those whose intellects are sharpened by well-considered reasoning.

Because, in the case of the opposite [of the probandum], the possibility of that suspicion is removed by the force of a subverting proof (*bādhakapramāṇa*). For instance, when non-existence is to be proven, existence is the counter-example (*vipakṣa*);
in that case, there must be the operation of perception (*pratyakṣavṛtti*).
For whatever possesses complete and unimpeded capacity at a given time, that necessarily comes into existence at that time;

for example, a sprout when the entire collection of its causes possesses unimpaired power. And since the totality of the eye and other factors is present, and the object to be seen exists, perceptual cognition—which has as its cause a capacity that is complete and unobstructed—necessarily arises. This is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason).

Therefore, since the reason (hetu) is excluded from the counter-position (vipakṣa) by the perception of its contradictory, it is pervaded by the fitness for the conventional designation of non-existence; thus, because the pervasion (vyāpti) is established, it is not inconclusive (anaikāntika).
Furthermore, because the connection with the intended probandum (sādhya) is established, any charge of contradiction (viruddhatā) has its impetuous onset utterly dispelled.

Therefore, since the reason is free from the stain of the suspicion that it is vitiated by fallacies such as being unestablished (*asiddha*), the non-existence of the universal is established once the matter at hand has been proven. Enough with this excessively prolix and digressive discourse; we shall desist. Furthermore, a universal is not the definition of an individual, as is the case with the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of a real entity.

Furthermore, the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) cannot consist of the phonemes and so forth that are both recurring and excluded, because it would follow that there would be a cognition with a fixed appearance of the phonemes and so forth [regardless of the individual].
If it is argued that this appearance belongs to the individual alone, then what else could be the recurring form of the universal?
Indeed, apart from the phonemes and the configuration (*saṃsthāna*), what other recurring entity exists?

If it is argued that the universal (*jāti*) and the individual (*vyakti*) are perceived through their mutual intermingling—due to the force of inherence (*samavāya*), such that their distinction is not manifested, like milk and water—then neither the form of the universal nor that of the particular has been grasped. Since there is no grasping of their own-nature (*svarūpa*), there is likewise no grasping of these two; thus, it has been demonstrated that such a cognition is ultimately without a real objective basis (*nirālambana*). Furthermore, that which is established by a cognition lacking an objective basis...

The universal [property] has been well-established; therefore, even though the qualified [subject] is unestablished, this reason is not unestablished. Furthermore, one should not consider it to be contradictory because it exists in the similar class (*sapakṣa*).
Nor does its inconclusiveness deserve even to be considered;
for non-perception of the perceptible is pervaded by independence from the linguistic convention of "non-existence. For if it were existent there, it would not fail to produce that convention.
In this case, there would be a dependence [on a further condition]:

namely, that by being excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa)—which is itself excluded by what is contradictory to the pervader—it comes to rest in the conventional usage of non-existence. Therefore, since non-perception is pervaded by that very conventional usage of non-existence, how could there be any inconclusiveness?
And thus, that very same point is established:
he who perceives a sixth common factor among these five fingers clearly manifest in direct perception while they are being pointed out, is like one who sees a horn growing upon his own head.
Thus [it is said].
And this is the ultimate meaning of everything previously stated:

a universal (*sāmānya*) situated within the five fingers appears on the path of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), yet it does not appear in that same way in a conceptualizing cognition (*vikalpākārabuddhi*).
For it is those very [fingers] that appear here with indistinct forms; therefore, there is no genus (*jāti*).
Furthermore, these two—perception and sound—are the causes of the error of similarity.
The direction for refuting the proof of universals has been set forth. // 3 //
This is the work of Paṇḍita Aśoka.
